sections.title: $Ax = \lambda x$: directions that $A$ only stretches
sections.summary: For $y' = Ay$, try $y = e^{\lambda t}x$: the exponential cancels and leaves $Ax = \lambda x$. An eigenvector keeps its direction under $A$, and $\lambda$ is the stretching factor. With two eigenvectors the solution is $c_1e^{\lambda_1t}x_1 + c_2e^{\lambda_2t}x_2$.
goals: Derive $Ax = \lambda x$ from the trial solution $e^{\lambda t}x$.
Find eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a $2\times2$ matrix.
Write the general solution of $y' = Ay$ and fit $y(0)$.
Know the eigenvalues of $A^2$, $A^n$ and $A + cI$.

notes.heading: From the equation to Ax = lambda x
paragraphs: A system $y' = Ay$ of $n$ equations couples the unknowns. Try the simplest possible solution, a fixed vector $x$ times a scalar exponential: $y = e^{\lambda t}x$. Then $y' = \lambda e^{\lambda t}x$ and $Ay = e^{\lambda t}Ax$. Cancel $e^{\lambda t}$: $Ax = \lambda x$.
So the right $x$ is a vector whose direction is unchanged by $A$; $\lambda$ is how much it is stretched (or shrunk, or reversed if negative).

notes.heading: The lecture's example
paragraphs: $y_1' = 5y_1 + y_2$, $y_2' = 3y_1 + 3y_2$, so $A = \begin{bmatrix}5 & 1\\ 3 & 3\end{bmatrix}$. The vector $x_1 = (1, 1)$ gives $Ax_1 = (6, 6) = 6x_1$, so $\lambda_1 = 6$. The vector $x_2 = (1, -3)$ gives $Ax_2 = (2, -6) = 2x_2$, so $\lambda_2 = 2$. The general solution is $y(t) = c_1e^{6t}(1, 1) + c_2e^{2t}(1, -3)$, and $y(0) = c_1(1,1) + c_2(1,-3)$ fixes the constants.

notes.heading: Simple consequences
paragraphs: If $Ax = \lambda x$ then $A^2x = \lambda^2x$ and $A^nx = \lambda^nx$: same eigenvectors, eigenvalues raised to the power ($36$ and $4$ for $A^2$ above). Also $(A + cI)x = (\lambda + c)x$: shifting by $cI$ shifts every eigenvalue by $c$.
A caution: the eigenvalues of $A + B$ are usually not the sums of eigenvalues of $A$ and $B$, because their eigenvectors are usually different.

example.answer: $\lambda = 5$ with $(1, 1)$ and $\lambda = 2$ with $(1, -2)$; the sum $7$ is the trace and the product $10$ the determinant.

sections.title: $A = V\Lambda V^{-1}$, powers $A^k$, and Markov matrices
sections.summary: Put the eigenvectors in the columns of $V$ and the eigenvalues in the diagonal $\Lambda$: $AV = V\Lambda$, so $A = V\Lambda V^{-1}$ and $A^k = V\Lambda^kV^{-1}$. For $u_{k+1} = Au_k$, write $u_0 = \sum c_ix_i$; then $u_k = \sum c_i\lambda_i^kx_i$. A Markov matrix has $\lambda = 1$ and its eigenvector is the steady state.
goals: Build $V$ and $\Lambda$ and check $AV = V\Lambda$.
Compute $A^k$ from $V\Lambda^kV^{-1}$.
Solve $u_{k+1} = Au_k$ with $c = V^{-1}u_0$.
Find the steady state of a Markov matrix.

notes.heading: Diagonalization
paragraphs: $A$ times each eigenvector column is $\lambda$ times that column: $AV = V\Lambda$ with $V = [x_1\ x_2\ \cdots]$ and $\Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \ldots)$. If the $n$ eigenvectors are independent, $V$ is invertible and $V^{-1}AV = \Lambda$, $A = V\Lambda V^{-1}$.

Then $A^2 = V\Lambda V^{-1}V\Lambda V^{-1} = V\Lambda^2V^{-1}$, and $A^k = V\Lambda^kV^{-1}$. Powers grow when some $|\lambda| > 1$, decay when every $|\lambda| < 1$, and $\lambda = 1$ gives a part that stays fixed. (A matrix without $n$ independent eigenvectors is called defective and cannot be diagonalized.)

notes.heading: Difference equations
paragraphs: $u_{k+1} = Au_k$ is the discrete twin of $y' = Ay$. Expand the start in eigenvectors, $u_0 = c_1x_1 + \cdots + c_nx_n$ (so $c = V^{-1}u_0$). Each piece is multiplied by its own $\lambda$ at each step: $u_k = c_1\lambda_1^kx_1 + \cdots + c_n\lambda_n^kx_n$.

notes.heading: Markov matrices
paragraphs: $A = \begin{bmatrix}0.8 & 0.3\\ 0.2 & 0.7\end{bmatrix}$ has nonnegative entries and columns adding to $1$. Its characteristic equation is $\lambda^2 - 1.5\lambda + 0.5 = (\lambda - 1)(\lambda - \tfrac12)$. For $\lambda = 1$: $x_1 = (0.6, 0.4)$ (check: $0.48 + 0.12 = 0.6$). For $\lambda = \tfrac12$: $x_2 = (1, -1)$.
So $u_k = c_1(0.6, 0.4) + c_2(\tfrac12)^k(1, -1) \to c_1(0.6, 0.4)$, the steady state. Google's PageRank is the steady state of a giant Markov matrix.

example.title: Following a Markov chain (authored)
example.problem: For the lecture's Markov matrix, find $u_k$ from $u_0 = (1, 0)$.
example.answer: $u_k = (0.6, 0.4) + 0.4(\tfrac12)^k(1, -1)$; the second part halves each step and the chain settles at $(0.6, 0.4)$.

Markov A = [.8 .3; .2 .7]: lambda 1, x (.6, .4); lambda 1/2, x (1, -1); steady state c1 (.6, .4). PageRank.

sections.title: Solving $y' = Ay$ with eigenvectors
sections.summary: $y(t) = c_1e^{\lambda_1t}x_1 + \cdots + c_ne^{\lambda_nt}x_n$ with $c = V^{-1}y(0)$. Stability requires every $\operatorname{Re}\lambda < 0$; an eigenvalue $0$ gives a steady state. For $A = \begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2\\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}$, $\lambda = 0$ and $-3$, and solutions approach a multiple of $(2, 1)$.
goals: Solve $y' = Ay$ from the eigenvalues and eigenvectors.
Relate stability to the real parts of the eigenvalues.
Use column sums: if every column of $A$ adds to $s$, then $s$ is an eigenvalue.

notes.heading: The solution
paragraphs: Each eigenvector solution $e^{\lambda_it}x_i$ solves $y' = Ay$, and so does any combination. Matching $y(0) = c_1x_1 + \cdots + c_nx_n$ means $Vc = y(0)$. The parts with $\operatorname{Re}\lambda < 0$ die out; parts with $\operatorname{Re}\lambda > 0$ blow up. Stability needs every real part negative.

notes.heading: Example
paragraphs: $A = \begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2\\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}$ has trace $-3$ and determinant $0$, so $\lambda = 0$ and $\lambda = -3$. For $\lambda = 0$: $Ax = 0$ gives $x_1 = (2, 1)$. For $\lambda = -3$: $x_2 = (1, -1)$. Then $y(t) = c_1(2, 1) + c_2e^{-3t}(1, -1) \to c_1(2, 1)$: a steady state (as for a Markov process in continuous time).

notes.heading: Column and row sums
paragraphs: Each column of this $A$ adds to $0$. In general, if every column adds to $s$, then $(1, \ldots, 1)A = s(1, \ldots, 1)$: $s$ is an eigenvalue of $A^T$, and $A$ and $A^T$ have the same eigenvalues (same determinant of $A - \lambda I$). If every row adds to $s$, then $A(1, \ldots, 1) = s(1, \ldots, 1)$ directly.

keyIdeas: Columns sum to $s$ $\Rightarrow$ $s$ is an eigenvalue.

sections.title: $e^{At}$, and matrices with the same eigenvalues
sections.summary: $e^{At} = I + At + \tfrac12(At)^2 + \cdots$ solves $Y' = AY$ with $Y(0) = I$, so $y(t) = e^{At}y(0)$, even for defective $A$. With eigenvectors, $e^{At} = Ve^{\Lambda t}V^{-1}$. Similar matrices $B = M^{-1}AM$ share eigenvalues; but $e^Ae^B \neq e^{A+B}$ unless $AB = BA$.
goals: Define $e^{At}$ by its series and differentiate it.
Compute $e^{At}$ for $A = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1\\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}$.
Use $e^{At} = Ve^{\Lambda t}V^{-1}$ when $A$ has $n$ eigenvectors.
Explain why similar matrices have the same eigenvalues.

notes.heading: The series
paragraphs: Copy the scalar series: $e^{At} = I + At + \dfrac{(At)^2}{2} + \dfrac{(At)^3}{6} + \cdots$. Differentiating term by term gives $A + A^2t + \tfrac12A^3t^2 + \cdots = Ae^{At}$. So $y(t) = e^{At}y(0)$ solves $y' = Ay$ for every square $A$, with or without a full set of eigenvectors.

notes.heading: Two ways to compute it
paragraphs: With $A = V\Lambda V^{-1}$, every power is $V\Lambda^kV^{-1}$, so the series collapses to $e^{At} = Ve^{\Lambda t}V^{-1}$, where $e^{\Lambda t}$ is diagonal with entries $e^{\lambda_it}$.

For the defective $A = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1\\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ (double eigenvalue $0$, only one eigenvector $(1, 0)$), $A^2 = 0$ and the series stops: $e^{At} = I + At = \begin{bmatrix}1 & t\\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$. In equations: $y_2' = 0$ keeps $y_2$ constant and $y_1' = y_2$ grows linearly, the factor $t$ again.

notes.heading: Similar matrices
paragraphs: $B = M^{-1}AM$ for an invertible $M$ is similar to $A$. If $Bx = \lambda x$ then $A(Mx) = \lambda(Mx)$: the same eigenvalues, with eigenvectors $Mx$. Strang's family $\begin{bmatrix}2&3\\0&4\end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&4\end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix}4&0\\0&2\end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix}0&2\\-4&6\end{bmatrix}$ all have $\lambda = 2, 4$ (trace $6$, determinant $8$).

Matrices with a repeated eigenvalue can fail to be similar: $\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix}$ is not similar to $2I$, since $M^{-1}(2I)M = 2I$ always. The best form for a defective matrix is the Jordan form.

A caution: $e^Ae^B$, $e^Be^A$ and $e^{A+B}$ differ in general; they agree when $AB = BA$. Likewise $y' = a(t)y$ has solution $e^{\int a}$, but for matrices $y' = A(t)y$ this fails unless the $A(t)$ commute.

sections.title: Symmetric $S$: real eigenvalues, orthogonal eigenvectors
sections.summary: A symmetric matrix $S = S^T$ has real eigenvalues and perpendicular eigenvectors, so $S = Q\Lambda Q^T$ with an orthogonal $Q$. Antisymmetric matrices have imaginary eigenvalues; orthogonal matrices have $|\lambda| = 1$. Complex vectors need the conjugate in the length: $\|x\|^2 = \bar{x}^Tx$.
goals: Find the eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors of $\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\1&3\end{bmatrix}$.
Write $S = Q\Lambda Q^T$.
Find eigenvalues of antisymmetric and orthogonal matrices.
Measure complex vectors with $\bar{x}^Tx$.

notes.heading: Symmetric matrices
paragraphs: $S = \begin{bmatrix}3 & 1\\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}$: $\lambda = 4$ with $(1, 1)$ and $\lambda = 2$ with $(1, -1)$. The eigenvalues are real and the eigenvectors are perpendicular: $(1,1)\cdot(1,-1) = 0$. This holds for every real symmetric matrix. Normalising the eigenvectors to unit length gives an orthogonal $Q$ ($Q^TQ = I$, so $Q^{-1} = Q^T$) and $S = Q\Lambda Q^T$.

notes.heading: Antisymmetric and orthogonal
paragraphs: $A = \begin{bmatrix}0 & -1\\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ has $A^T = -A$. Its equation $\lambda^2 + 1 = 0$ gives $\lambda = \pm i$, with eigenvectors $(1, -i)$ and $(1, i)$: purely imaginary eigenvalues. Adding $3I$: $\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1\\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}$ has $\lambda = 3 \pm i$.

The rotation by $45°$, $Q = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1\\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$, is orthogonal; its eigenvalues $\tfrac{1 \pm i}{\sqrt2}$ have absolute value $1$, as for every orthogonal matrix: $Q$ preserves lengths, so it cannot stretch an eigenvector.

notes.heading: Complex lengths
paragraphs: For $\lambda = a + ib$, $|\lambda|^2 = \lambda\bar\lambda = a^2 + b^2$. For a complex vector the length squared is $\bar{x}^Tx = |x_1|^2 + \cdots + |x_n|^2$; plain $x^Tx$ can be zero, as for $(1, i)$. Complex matrices with $\bar{S}^T = S$ (Hermitian) behave like real symmetric ones: real eigenvalues, orthogonal eigenvectors.

example.title: Spectral form of a symmetric matrix (authored)
example.answer: $S = Q\Lambda Q^T$ with $\Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(3, 1)$; the columns of $Q$ are perpendicular unit vectors.

Q = (1/sqrt2)[1 -1; 1 1]: (1 +- i)/sqrt2, |lambda| = 1. |lambda|^2 = a^2 + b^2; complex length x-bar^T x. Hermitian: real eigenvalues.

sections.title: Oscillating systems $My'' + Ky = 0$
sections.summary: Masses and springs give $My'' + Ky = 0$. Pure oscillations $y = (\cos\omega t)x$ require $Kx = \omega^2Mx$: the eigenvalues are squared frequencies, and the eigenvectors are the mode shapes. For $y'' + \tfrac{k}{m}\begin{bmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{bmatrix}y = 0$ the modes are $(1, 1)$ with $\omega^2 = k/m$ and $(1, -1)$ with $\omega^2 = 3k/m$.
goals: Turn $My'' + Ky = 0$ into the eigenvalue problem $Kx = \omega^2Mx$.
Find the two modes of a two-mass system.
Write the solution from $y(0)$ and $y'(0)$ as a sum of modes.

notes.heading: Modes
paragraphs: Newton's law for $n$ masses connected by springs is $My'' + Ky = 0$, with a diagonal mass matrix $M$ and a symmetric stiffness matrix $K$. Try $y = e^{i\omega t}x$: $-\omega^2Mx + Kx = 0$, that is $Kx = \omega^2Mx$. Each eigenvector $x_i$ is a mode shape, and $\omega_i$ its frequency.
Since there are $2n$ initial values ($y(0)$ and $y'(0)$), the solution is $y(t) = \sum (A_i\cos\omega_it + B_i\sin\omega_it)\,x_i$. Starting from rest ($y'(0) = 0$) all $B_i = 0$.

notes.heading: Two masses
paragraphs: Equal masses $m$ between three springs $k$ (fixed at both ends): $y'' + \tfrac{k}{m}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1\\ -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}y = 0$. The matrix has trace $4$ and determinant $3$, so its eigenvalues are $1$ and $3$, giving $\omega^2 = k/m$ and $3k/m$. The slow mode $(1, 1)$ moves both masses together; the fast mode $(1, -1)$ moves them against each other.
From rest: $y(t) = A_1\cos\left(\sqrt{k/m}\,t\right)(1, 1) + A_2\cos\left(\sqrt{3k/m}\,t\right)(1, -1)$.

keyIdeas: Eigenvalues = squared frequencies; eigenvectors = mode shapes.

example.title: Pull one mass and let go (authored)

steps.text: Each mode oscillates at its own frequency (from rest: cosines).

example.answer: $y_1 = \tfrac12(\cos t + \cos\sqrt3t)$ and $y_2 = \tfrac12(\cos t - \cos\sqrt3t)$: the energy moves back and forth between the masses.
